items.stem: As used in the second sentence, the word “vacant” most nearly means:

Physically unoccupied by buildings or structures

items.stimulus:
In a climate-controlled room at the city museum, curator Lena Ortiz studies a 1798 map of the river district. Its blank margins are not vacant, she argues, because they contain no buildings; they are vacant because the survey records no claims about who used the land. At first glance, the map’s geometric avenues and carefully lettered labels seem to promise an orderly account of the district. Yet Ortiz argues that the omission of informal paths is not neutrality but a choice that gives the drawn streets an exaggerated currency.

When conservators lifted a later backing from the map, they found faint pencil marks describing a ferry crossing and a seasonal market. The discovery tempered Ortiz’s initial confidence that the map’s silence had been deliberate from the start. She began to read the document less as a picture of the district than as a negotiation among surveyors, property owners, and later editors. The legend appears to reserve its warmest adjective, “improved,” for avenues favored by investors, while calling the market’s irregular lane merely “convenient.”

At the exhibition, Ortiz places the official map beside a translucent enlargement of the pencil marks, making both systems of value legible without declaring either complete. Rather than render the map’s inconsistencies as errors to be corrected, she presents them as evidence of changing ideas about what a city ought to display. This arrangement channels the visitor’s attention from the map’s apparent precision toward the decisions that produced it. The map thus yields not a single stable portrait of the district but a record of the pressures that shaped its surface.
